Write what you'd make if the whole batch sells.
proof: Your cost sheet with your price and break-even number.

title: Check Your Pay Stub
short: Check your latest pay stub against your own hours and write what each deduction is.
why: Payroll mistakes happen and nobody checks for you. Knowing each line also explains why your check is less than hours times pay.
how: Compare the hours on your stub with the hours you logged.
Write what each deduction is in your own words: income tax, Social Security, Medicare.
If the hours don't match, write down the dates and take them to your manager.
proof: Your handwritten notes. Don't photograph the stub.

title: Get Your Tax Back
short: Find out if you can get back the tax taken from your pay, even if you didn't have to file.
why: If income tax came out of your pay and you didn't earn much, you may get some or all of it back, but only if you file.
how: Search "IRS do I need to file" and use the official tool on irs.gov.
Look up the free filing options on irs.gov.
Write whether you need to file, whether to file anyway, and the deadline.
Missed a year? You can usually still claim a refund up to three years back.
proof: Your notes: file or not, the free option and the deadline.

title: Compare Savings Accounts
short: Compare savings accounts at two banks or credit unions and write which one you'd pick.
why: Some accounts charge monthly fees or pay almost nothing. Twenty minutes comparing keeps more of your money yours.
how: Pick one bank and one credit union, local or online.
For each, write the monthly fee, the minimum to keep in, the interest rate and ID needed.
Circle the one you'd pick and write why.
proof: Your comparison on paper. No account details.

title: Mock Interview
short: Have someone you know ask you five common interview questions while you answer out loud.
why: Interviews go better when you've already heard yourself answer. Practicing with a real person shows where you ramble or go blank.
how: Write five: about you, why this job, a strength, a problem you solved, when you can work.
Hand them to a parent, friend or coworker and start the 20:00 timer.
Answer out loud with real examples from school, work, sports or your projects.
Write one thing to fix for each answer.
proof: Your question list with notes on what to fix.

title: Line Up a Reference
short: Ask a teacher, coach or past boss in person if they'll be a reference for your applications.
why: Many applications ask for references. Asking first means you have a name ready, and they know the call is coming.
how: Pick an adult who's seen you work: a teacher, coach, past boss or volunteer leader.
Ask in person if they'd be a reference, and tell them what you're applying for.
Write their title and how they want to be contacted on your job list.
Never list someone who hasn't said yes.
proof: Your reference note with their name and contact details covered.

title: Find a Volunteer Spot
short: Find one volunteer role near you that takes people your age, and write how to sign up.
why: It's real experience before you're old enough for most jobs, and it gives you a resume line and a reference.
how: Search "volunteer" plus your town and age, or ask at a library, shelter or food bank.
Check the minimum age and whether a parent has to sign or come with you.
Write the place, the role, the hours and the next step to sign up.
Under 18, get a parent's OK before you sign up.
proof: Your notes: the place, the role, the hours and how to sign up.

title: Check Your Credit Report
short: Get your free credit report and check that every account on it is really yours.
why: An account you didn't open can block a lease or a phone plan later. The report is free, and checking it takes minutes.
how: Go to annualcreditreport.com, the free official site. Don't use look-alike sites.
Get your report from one of the three bureaus and read every account on it.
Write on paper whether it all looks right, and anything you don't recognize.
No report found? That's normal if you've never had credit. Write that down.
proof: Your handwritten notes. Never the report itself.

title: Apply
short: Send one complete application for a job, internship or scholarship today.
why: Most applications never get a reply. The people with offers are the ones who keep sending them.
how: Pick one you qualify for from your list, or find one now.
Fill in every field and attach your resume if they ask for one.
Apply on a laptop if you can. Read it through once more, then send it.
Never pay to apply.
proof: The confirmation on a laptop or other screen, private info covered.

title: Write Your First Resume
short: Write a complete one-page resume today, even if it's short.
why: A short resume beats none. Jobs, programs and scholarships all ask for one, and fixing a page is much easier than starting it.
how: On a laptop or by hand, start with your name, contact details, and school or work.
Add teams, clubs, volunteering, projects, side jobs and skills, with numbers if you can.
Keep it to one page, a plain font and no photo.
Cover your name and contact details before the photo.
proof: The full page on paper or a laptop, name and contact covered.

title: Walk In and Ask
short: Go into one place that hires people your age and ask the manager if they're hiring.
why: Local shops and restaurants often hire people who ask in person. Showing up makes you a real person to them, not one more online form.
how: Pick a place you can get to and go at a quiet time, not the lunch rush.
Ask for the manager, say you're looking for work and when you're free.
Take an application or ask how to apply, and write down the next step.
Never pay to apply.
proof: The application or your notes, personal details covered.

title: Sell What You Don't Use
short: List one thing you don't use for sale today, with real photos and a price based on sold listings.
why: Selling stuff you already own is the easiest first sale there is. You learn photos, pricing and honest descriptions along the way.
how: Clean it, find its box, charger or tags, then shoot it in daylight: front, back, flaws.
Price it from sold listings and write an honest description.
18 or older, list it on a site that ships. Under 18, a parent lists it and answers buyers.
Ship it so you never meet a buyer, and never take payment off the site.
proof: Your listing on a laptop or other screen, personal details covered.

title: Earn It at Home
short: Offer to do one big job at home beyond your normal chores for a set price, then do all of it.
why: It's the easiest first paid job to get: no commute, no application. You still learn the real thing: agree on a price, then deliver.
how: Pick something bigger than chores: clear the garage, weed the yard, wash inside windows.
Offer it to a parent or relative with a price and a time it'll be done.
Do the whole job, then show them the result before you get paid.
No ladders, power tools or strong cleaning chemicals.
proof: The job before and after, no people in the photo.

title: Build a Budget Sheet
short: Build a free spreadsheet for money in, money out and savings, and fill in this month.
why: A sheet that adds itself up shows where the month went at a glance. Spreadsheets are also a skill almost every job uses.
how: On a laptop or computer, open a free spreadsheet: date, what, in, out, category.
Fill in this month from your spending lists, receipts and order history.
Total each column with SUM, then total each category to find the biggest.
Circle the category you'll cut next month.
proof: Your sheet on a computer screen with totals, details covered.

title: Make a Work Sample
short: Pick one job or gig you'd want and make a small sample that proves you can do its main task.
why: Saying you can do something is easy. A sample made for that exact role shows it, and you can attach it when you apply.
how: Pick a real posting, now or for later: design, video editing, spreadsheets, tutoring.
Find the main task it asks for.
Make one small version: a flyer, a 30-second edit, a sample spreadsheet, a lesson plan.
Save it somewhere you can attach it from.
proof: Your finished sample, on paper or on a laptop screen.

title: Shop Under Budget
short: Take a real shopping list and a set budget, and get everything on it for less.
why: Unit prices and store brands are where everyday savings are. One real list is the quickest way to learn to read them.
how: Get the list and budget from whoever pays, and go with them if you can't get there alone.
In the store or on a grocery site, compare the unit price, not the package price.
Pick the store brand wherever it's the same thing.
Write the budget, the total and what you saved on the list.
proof: Your list with the budget and total, next to the groceries or cart.

title: Ask for the Raise
short: Write your case for more pay, then ask your manager for it, with a number.
why: Raises often go to people who ask with reasons, not the ones who wait to be noticed. A written case keeps you calm and specific.
how: Write how long you've worked there and what you do beyond the basics.
Add proof: shifts covered, people trained, extra tasks, good feedback.
Ask your manager for five minutes, make your case and name a number.
Write their answer. If it's a no, ask what would make it a yes and when to ask again.
proof: Your written case with your manager's answer added. No names.

title: Financial Aid: 45 Minutes
short: 45 minutes on your FAFSA or your college or program's financial aid forms.
why: These forms decide how much school costs you, and some aid runs out. Finishing early can mean more money.
how: Gather what the form asks for, with a parent or guardian if it needs their info.
Start the 45:00 timer and work through the next section.
Before you stop, list on paper the sections done, what's left and the deadline.
The FAFSA is free. Never pay a site to file it for you.
proof: Your checklist of the sections you finished. Not the form.

title: Do One Paid Job
short: Do one paid job for a neighbor or family friend you know, at a price agreed before you start.
why: Getting paid by someone outside your home is a real first job, and one job done well is how the next one finds you.
how: Pick one: yard work, pet sitting, washing a car, tech setup, moving boxes.
Under 18, only work for people your family knows, and only with a parent's OK.
Agree on the price and what done looks like before you start.
Do all of it, then show them the result before you get paid.
proof: The finished job, no people in the photo.

title: Ask About Their Job
short: Ask an adult you know three real questions about their job, in person, and write the answers.
why: Job titles don't tell you what the work is like. Ten minutes with someone who does it tells you more than an hour of videos.
how: Pick someone with a job you're curious about: a relative, coach, teacher or family friend.
Write three questions: a normal day, what they'd learn first, what they'd do differently.
Ask in person, listen, and write the answers right after.
proof: Your three questions and their answers, no names.

title: Follow Up
short: Call or email about one application you sent 5 or more days ago, and write down the answer.
why: A lot of applications sit unread. A short, polite check-in puts your name back in front of them and gets you a real answer.
how: Pick one application from your job list with no reply after 5 to 10 days.
Write what to say: your name, the role, when you applied, that you're still interested.
Call at a quiet time or email the hiring contact, and keep it short.
Write the date and their answer on your job list. Never pay to apply.
proof: The date and answer on your job list, personal details covered.

title: Create 1 Thing
short: Make one small, finished thing in 15 minutes: a sketch, a verse, a loop, a logo, a paragraph.
why: Making something small most days beats waiting for a big idea. You get quicker, and you end up with a pile of work to pick from.
how: Pick the format: sketch, verse, beat loop, layout, a few lines of code.
Give it 15 minutes and finish it, even if it's rough.
Date it or name it so you can find it later.
proof: The finished thing, on paper or another device's screen.

title: 15 Minutes of Reps
short: Drill one basic of your skill for 15 minutes: scales, gesture sketches, lettering, code exercises.
why: The basics are what make everything else look good. Short reps most days add up quicker than one long session a month.
how: Pick the one basic you're weakest at.
Start the 15:00 timer and repeat it until the timer ends.
Circle or save your best rep.
proof: Your page of reps, your instrument or your practice setup.

title: Improve Yesterday's Work
short: Take something you made in the last few days and make its weakest part better.
why: Most good work is okay work that got fixed a few times. A day away gives you the fresh eyes to see what to fix.
how: Photograph it the way it looks now.
Find the one part that looks or sounds weakest.
Fix only that part, then photograph it again.
proof: The piece before and after the fix.

title: 5 Rough Versions
short: Make five quick, rough versions of one idea, then circle the best one.
why: Your first idea is rarely your best. Five quick tries show you options you wouldn't have thought of.
how: Pick one thing: a logo, a tee graphic, a layout, a video hook, a chorus.
Make five rough versions, about two minutes each.
Circle the strongest and write one line on why.
proof: All five versions with the best one circled.

title: Pick 5 References
short: Find five pieces by other people that look or sound the way you want your next piece to.
why: Pros collect references before they start. It turns "I want it to look good" into something you can actually aim at.
how: Find five images, tracks or pages close to what you want to make next.
List them on paper: who made it and what it's called.
Next to each, write the one thing you'd take from it.
Star the one closest to what you're making next.
proof: Your handwritten list of five, with a note on each.

title: Write Your Two-Line Bio
short: Write two lines on what you make and who it's for, ready for a portfolio, shop or profile.
why: When someone asks what you make, you'll have a real answer instead of "oh, just stuff." It goes straight on a portfolio or shop too.
how: Line one: what you make, in plain words.
Line two: who it's for, or what makes yours different.
Read it out loud and cut every word you don't need.
proof: Your two lines, written down.

title: Price One Thing
short: Work out a real price for one thing you make or could do, with the math on paper.
why: Guessed prices are almost always too low. Adding up materials and time shows what one actually costs you to make.
how: List what the materials for one cost.
Time how long one takes and pay yourself at least minimum wage for it.
Add it up, check what one similar thing sells for, and pick your price.
proof: Your cost list and final price on paper.

title: Shoot It Like a Product
short: Take a clean, well-lit photo of one thing you made, like it's going in a shop.
why: People judge work by its photo first. Daylight and a plain background make good work look professional.
how: Set it by a window in daylight, on a plain wall, sheet or paper.
Wipe the lens, shoot it straight on, then from an angle.
Keep the best shot in your work folder.
proof: Your best shot of the piece on a plain background.

title: Set a Finish Date
short: Pick the date your current project will be done, write it down and tell one person.
why: Projects with no date stay "almost done" for months. Once someone else knows the date, it's harder to let it slide.
how: Pick a date one to four weeks out that's tight but doable.
Write the date and one line on what "done" means.
Tell one person you know and ask them to check in on that day.
proof: The date and your one-line "done", written down.

title: Break Down a Pro Piece
short: Pick one piece by someone great at your skill and write 3 things they did on purpose.
why: Good work looks easy until you spot the choices behind it. Once you can name them, you can use them.
how: Pick one piece you wish you'd made: a song, a poster, a video, a comic page.
Look at it or listen to it slowly, twice.
Write 3 choices they made on purpose: color, timing, layout, sound.
proof: Your 3 notes, with the name of the piece.

title: Learn 3 Shortcuts
short: Learn three shortcuts in the app you make things in and write them on a note by your screen.
why: Shortcuts save a few seconds every time, and you use them all session. They're a big part of why good editors and coders seem so quick.
how: Pick the app you use most: a video editor, a drawing app, a music app, a code editor.
Look up its shortcuts and pick three for things you do all the time.
Write them on a sticky note, put it by your screen and use each one today.
proof: Your shortcut note, stuck by your screen.

title: 10 Ideas, Pick One
short: Write 10 ideas for things you could make next, then star the one you'll start this week.
why: Waiting for an idea rarely works. Writing ten does: the first few are obvious, and the good ones show up near the end.
how: Give yourself 10 minutes and write 10 ideas, bad ones included.
Make each one specific: "a 30-second stop-motion of my sneakers", not "a video".
Star the one you'll start this week and write its first step next to it.
proof: Your list of 10, with one starred.

title: Cut It to Version One
short: List everything your project is meant to have, then cut it until version one fits in two weeks.
why: Most apps, games and brands never come out because the plan is too big. A small version that's finished beats a huge one that isn't.
how: List every feature, page, product or level you've planned.
Cross out anything people could live without in the first version.
Keep cutting until what's left fits in two weeks of your real free time.
proof: Your list with the cuts crossed out.

title: Build for 30
short: Phone away. 30 minutes on the thing you're making.
why: Projects move in focused sessions, not in thinking about them. 30 minutes most days is enough to finish real things.
how: Decide what you'll work on before the timer starts.
Put your phone in another room or out of reach.
Start the 30:00 timer and don't switch to anything else until it ends.
proof: Your work or workspace after the timer.

title: Learn One Tool
short: Spend 20 minutes learning one tool or technique you don't know yet, then use it once.
why: Every new tool makes the next piece quicker or better. 20 minutes gets you past the confusing first part.
how: Pick one: an app feature, a brush, a chord, a stitch, a code function.
Start the 20:00 timer and follow one free tutorial or guide.
Use it once on something of your own before you stop.
proof: What you made with the new tool, next to your notes.

title: Ship Something
short: Stop planning. Finish one part of your project today: a page, a design, a feature, a track.
why: Planning feels like progress, but nothing exists at the end of it. A finished part is something you can show, test or sell.
how: Pick the smallest part that would count as done.
Work on it until it's finished, not until it's perfect.
Save it, export it or put it where it belongs in the project.
proof: The finished part, on paper or another device's screen.

title: Rough Draft, No Undo
short: Make a whole rough draft in 20 minutes without fixing anything.
why: Fixing as you go is why drafts never get finished. A full bad draft is easy to improve. Half a perfect one isn't.
how: Pick the piece: a story, a song, a design, a video plan, a pitch.
Start the 20:00 timer and go from start to end.
No deleting, no undo. Mark problems with an X and keep going.
proof: The messy draft, start to finish.

title: Copy to Learn
short: Recreate one short piece by someone better than you, slowly, to see how they did it.
why: Artists, musicians and coders all learn by copying. Your hands figure out things your eyes skip.
how: Pick a short piece: a drawing, a riff, a layout, a page of code.
Copy it slowly, one part at a time.
Write two things you noticed that you'll use in your own work.
Keep it as practice. Never sell it or call it yours.
proof: Your copy next to your two notes.

title: Make It With Limits
short: Make one piece with three rules, like three colors, one instrument, 100 words or 30 seconds.
why: Limits get you past the blank page. When you can't do everything, you start making choices quickly.
how: Write three rules before you start.
Make one complete piece that follows all three.
Write the rules next to the finished piece.
proof: The finished piece with your three rules beside it.

title: Plan It on One Page
short: Put your project on one page: what it is, who it's for, the steps, the cost, the first move.
why: A plan that fits on one page actually gets used. It also shows what you're missing before you spend any money.
how: Write what it is and who it's for at the top.
List every step to a first finished version.
Add what it will cost, then circle the first step and do it this week.
proof: Your one-page plan.

title: Mock It Up
short: Put your design on the real thing: a tee template, a poster on a wall, a sticker on a laptop.
why: A design on a blank page is hard to judge. Seeing it in place shows what works, and lets other people picture it.
how: Pick one design or piece you've made.
Draw it onto a printed template, or drop it into a free mockup site.
Make one change the mockup showed you, then save it.
proof: The finished mockup, on paper or another device's screen.

title: Make Your Price List
short: Make one page that lists what you sell or do, the prices, and how to order.
why: People who might buy won't ask twice. A page with clear prices and how to order makes it easy to say yes.
how: List each thing you offer with its price.
Add one line on what's included and how long it takes.
Add how to order: no home details, and under 18 use a contact a parent OKs.
proof: Your price list, personal details covered.

title: Make a Brand Kit
short: Pick two or three colors, one or two fonts and a rough logo for your project, all on one page.
why: A consistent look is what makes a few pieces feel like a brand or a body of work instead of random stuff.
how: Pull colors and type from your references or your best pieces.
Put the colors, the fonts and a rough logo on one page.
Use that page for everything you make for this project.
proof: Your brand kit, on paper or another device's screen.

title: Pick Your Best 3
short: Choose your three best pieces, put them in one folder, and write why each one works.
why: Knowing which work is your best tells you what to make more of. It's also the start of any portfolio or shop.
how: Look through everything you've made in the last few months.
Pick three and put them in one folder or album.
Write one line for each: what makes it good.
proof: Your three picks, or a list of them, with your lines on each.

title: Make It for Someone
short: Make one thing today for someone you know that they'll use: a card, a flyer, a cover, a fix.
why: Making for a real person means you have to finish it and get it right for them, not just for you.
how: Pick someone and something they'd use: a birthday card, a flyer, a playlist cover.
Make it today, start to finish.
Give it to them and write down what they said.
proof: The finished piece, no names or personal details shown.

title: Make Something for Work
short: Use your skill to fix one thing at work: a sign, a checklist, a how-to sheet, a menu board.
why: A clearer sign or checklist makes every shift easier, and it's real work you can talk about in your next interview.
how: Spot one thing at work that's messy, unclear or hard to read.
Ask your manager if you can redo it, and if a photo of it is OK.
Make it, show them, and keep the photo for your portfolio.
proof: The finished piece, with no customer or coworker info shown.

title: Use It on Schoolwork
short: Use your skill on one school assignment: design the slides, edit the video, build the poster.
why: School projects are free practice with a deadline. Doing them with your real skill gives you work worth keeping.
how: Pick an assignment due in the next two weeks.
Decide which part your skill would make better.
Make that part as well as you can and save a copy for your portfolio.
proof: The piece you made, with names and scores hidden.

title: Find the Name
short: Write 20 names for your brand or project, cut to two, and check neither is already taken.
why: The first name you think of is usually the obvious one. Twenty gets you better options, and checking now saves a rename later.
how: Write 20 names in 10 minutes, bad ones included.
Cross names out until two are left.
Search both to see if a brand or product already uses them.
proof: Your list of 20 with the final two circled.

title: Make It With Someone
short: Make something with a friend in one sitting: a track, a short video, a design, a game level.
why: Working with someone shows you new ways to do things, and it's harder to quit halfway when someone is counting on you.
how: Invite someone you know who makes things too.
Agree on one small thing you can finish together today.
Split the parts and put it together before you stop.
proof: What you made together, with no people in the photo.

title: Make a Series of 3
short: Make three small pieces that clearly belong together: same theme, same style.
why: Brands, shows and portfolios are built on sets, not one-offs. Three that match look like a plan.
how: Pick one theme and one style rule.
Make three small pieces that follow both.
Lay them side by side and fix the one that doesn't fit.
proof: All three pieces side by side.

title: Get Set Up
short: Pick one skill to start, set up one free tool for it, and make a test piece today.
why: Setup is where a lot of people quit before they start. Get it done in one go, and next time you just open it and make something.
how: Pick one skill to start: drawing, beats, video, code, design or writing.
Find one free app or tool for it and set it up. Skip anything that asks for a card.
Make a 5-minute test piece with it and save it.
proof: Your test piece, or a note of the tool and what you made.

title: Fix the Hardest Part
short: 20 minutes on only the hardest part of what you're working on, done slowly.
why: Starting from the top every time means you mostly practice what you can already do. Slow reps on the hard part fix it.
how: Pick the one spot that keeps going wrong: four bars, the hands, a trick, a transition.
Start the 20:00 timer and work only on that spot, slower than feels normal.
Speed up only once you get it right three times in a row.
proof: Your practice page, instrument or setup after the timer.

title: Record It, Fix Two Things
short: Record one run of what you're practicing, play it back, and write down two things to fix.
why: You can't see or hear your own mistakes while you're doing it. One playback shows what feels fine but isn't.
how: Record one full run on your phone: a song, a set, a speech, a routine.
Play it back once, all the way through, without stopping.
Write the two changes that would make the biggest difference.
Start your next practice on the first one.
proof: Your two fixes, written down.

title: 500 New Words
short: Write 500 new words of your story, script, fan fiction or blog.
why: Writers get better by finishing pages, not by rereading the first one. 500 words is enough to move a story forward.
how: Open where you left off. Don't reread more than the last paragraph.
Write until you hit 500 new words. No editing until then.
Write the word count at the bottom.
proof: Your new pages with the word count, on paper or another screen.

title: Write Up One Project
short: Write 150 words on one thing you made: what it was, what you did, and what you'd change.
why: When a client, teacher or interviewer asks about your work, this is your answer. One clear write-up says more than ten pictures.
how: Pick one finished piece you're proud of.
Write what it was for, what you did and the hardest part.
Add one thing you'd change next time. Keep it under 150 words.
proof: Your 150-word write-up.

title: One-Hour Build
short: Make one complete thing in 60 minutes: a poster, a one-page site, a short video, a song sketch.
why: A hard time limit makes you finish instead of polish. One finished thing teaches you more than five started ones.
how: Decide the thing and what "done" means before you start.
Phone away. Start the 60:00 timer.
Spend the last 10 minutes finishing, not adding.
proof: The finished thing when the timer ends.

title: Finish a Full Tutorial
short: Follow one free tutorial all the way to the end and make the thing it teaches.
why: Most people quit tutorials halfway. Finishing one gives you a real result and a skill you can reuse in your own work.
how: Pick one free tutorial that's 20 to 40 minutes long.
Pause after each step and do it yourself before moving on.
Change one thing at the end so the result is yours.
proof: The thing you made from the tutorial.

title: Redo an Old Piece
short: Remake something you made months ago from scratch, then compare the two.
why: Progress is hard to see day to day. The old and new versions side by side show exactly how much you've improved.
how: Photograph the old piece first.
Remake it from scratch without copying the old one.
Photograph the new one and write one line on what changed.
proof: The old piece, then the new one.

title: Watch 3 People Try It
short: Have three people you know try what you made while you watch and stay quiet.
why: People won't tell you where they got confused, but you'll see it. Three tries show you what to fix first.
how: Pick something people can use: a game level, an app, a site, a zine, a board game.
Hand it over without explaining. Watch, don't help.
Write down every spot where they pause, get stuck or ask a question.
Circle any problem that happened more than once.
proof: Your notes from all three tries, no names.

title: Sell One Thing
short: Offer one thing you made to people you know until one buys it or three say no.
why: The first sale teaches you more about pricing and pitching than any video. One yes also tells you people want it.
how: Pick one finished piece and set the price before you ask.
Offer it in person or by message to people you know.
Write down each answer and what they said about the price.
Under 18? Take cash or let a parent handle payment. Never share bank details.
proof: Your sale note: item, price and answers, no names.

title: Submit Your Work
short: Enter one piece into a contest, showcase, talent show, zine or school exhibit before its deadline.
why: Work kept in a folder never gets a chance. Someone else's deadline pushes you to finish, and some entries win.
how: Find a free one: ask a teacher, or check your school, library or local rec center.
Pick your best piece that fits the rules and polish it.
Under 18? Get a parent's OK first. Never pay to enter.
Submit it before the deadline.
proof: Your entry confirmation on paper or another screen, details covered.

title: Build a Portfolio Page
short: Make one page or PDF with your best three to five pieces, a title and one line on each.
why: When someone asks to see your work, one link or PDF beats scrolling through your camera roll. It's what gets you picked or paid.
how: Use a free site builder, a doc or a slide.
Add your best three to five pieces with one line each.
First name and an email only. No phone number, school name or photos of you.
Open it on your phone and fix anything that looks off.
proof: Your portfolio on a laptop, tablet or printout, details covered.

title: Finish What You Dropped
short: Pick one piece you started and abandoned, and finish it today.
why: Half-done work keeps nagging you. Finishing it gives you one more real piece instead of another thing you almost made.
how: Photograph it as you left it.
Decide what "done" means and cut anything extra.
Finish it and photograph the result.
proof: The piece as you left it, then finished.

title: Start It Today
short: Take the project you keep talking about and make its first real piece today.
why: An idea stays an idea until the first file, sketch or page exists. After that you're fixing something real, not wondering.
how: Set it up: name the folder, open a new page, get the materials out.
Make the first real piece: a sketch, a page, a beat, a first screen.
Write the next step before you stop.
proof: The first piece of the project.

title: Get Paid for Your Skill
short: Offer your skill for pay to people you know until one says yes or three say no.
why: One paid job teaches pricing, deadlines and working for someone else. It's also something real to point to when you ask for the next one.
how: Pick one job you do well, like a design, an edit, a lesson or a repair, and set a price.
Offer it to relatives or family friends. If you're under 18, tell a parent first.
On a yes, write the job, date and price on paper and get their OK before you start.
proof: The answers you got, or the agreed job and price, on paper, no names.

title: Make the Bed
short: Make your bed before you leave the room this morning.
why: It's harder to crawl back into a made bed, and one thing in your room is done before the day even starts.
how: Do it right after you get up, before you check your phone.
Pull the sheet and covers up and smooth them flat.
Pillow on top. It doesn't need to look like a hotel.
proof: Your made bed.

title: 10-Minute Room Reset
short: Reset one part of your room in 10 minutes: the floor, desk, closet or by the bed.
why: You don't need a free Saturday to fix your room. Ten minutes on one zone keeps it from turning into a weekend job.
how: Pick one zone: the floor, the desk, the closet floor or next to the bed.
Start the 10:00 timer.
Trash out, dishes out, clothes in the hamper or away, the rest where it lives.
Done when the timer ends. Keep going only if you want to.
proof: The zone you reset, after the timer.

title: Clear One Surface
short: Clear one dresser, nightstand, counter or table until only what belongs there is left.
why: Clutter grows on the surface that's already covered. Clear one and you have somewhere to work, eat or drop your stuff.
how: Pick the dresser, nightstand, counter or table that bugs you most.
Take the before photo, then take everything off it.
Trash out, dishes to the kitchen, the rest where it lives. Wipe it down.
Put back only what you use there.
proof: The surface before, then cleared.

title: Tomorrow Is Ready
short: Tonight, lay out tomorrow's outfit, set your alarm and plug in everything that needs charging.
why: Mornings go wrong when you're hunting for a charger or a clean shirt. Ten minutes tonight and you just get up and go.
how: Lay out tomorrow's whole outfit, shoes included.
Plug in your phone, earbuds and anything else that needs charging.
Set your alarm and check tomorrow's first thing: what time, where, what to bring.
Keys, ID and bus pass go in their spot by the door.
proof: Tomorrow's outfit laid out, with your stuff charging.

title: Return Every Cup
short: Get every cup, plate, bowl and wrapper out of your room, and the dishes washed or loaded.
why: Dishes in your room turn into smells, bugs and an argument. It's a few minutes if you do it before they pile up.
how: Check the desk, the floor, next to the bed and inside your bag.
Wrappers and cans go straight in the trash or recycling.
Wash the dishes, or rinse and load the dishwasher. Don't leave them in the sink.
proof: Everything you collected, washed or in the dishwasher.

title: Give It Back
short: Find one thing you borrowed and pack it to return today or tomorrow.
why: The longer you keep it, the more awkward it gets to return. Packing it now takes it off your mind and keeps people willing to lend.
how: Look for books, chargers, clothes, games or tools that aren't yours. Library books count.
Put it in your bag or by the door so it leaves with you.
Won't see them soon? Text them the day you'll bring it.
proof: The borrowed thing, packed to give back.

title: Unsubscribe From 5
short: On a laptop or computer, unsubscribe from 5 email lists that only send you ads.
why: Promo emails bury the ones that matter: school, work, applications. Five fewer senders is less to dig through every day.
how: Open your email on a laptop or computer and search for the word unsubscribe.
Pick five senders you never open and use the Unsubscribe button by their name.
Sketchy-looking sender? Don't click anything inside. Mark it as spam instead.
Delete what they already sent while you're there.
proof: An unsubscribe confirmation on a laptop screen, your email covered.

title: Bag Dump
short: Empty your gym bag, work bag or everyday bag completely and repack only what you need.
why: Bags collect old papers, wrappers and lost stuff. Dumping it out is how you find the missing charger and stop carrying junk.
how: Turn the bag upside down and empty every pocket.
Trash out, papers sorted, lost stuff back where it lives.
Shake it out or wipe the inside.
Repack only what you need this week.
proof: The full dump with cards turned over, then just what goes back in.

title: Change Your Sheets
short: Strip your bed and put on clean sheets and a clean pillowcase.
why: Sheets hold sweat and dust, and after a while your room starts to smell like it. Every week or two is the normal swap.
how: Pull off the sheets and pillowcases, then take the before photo.
Put on a clean fitted sheet, top sheet or cover, and pillowcase.
Start the wash now, or put the old set in the hamper.
Only one set? Wash and dry it now and put it back on tonight.
proof: The bare mattress, then the bed with clean sheets on.

title: One Spot for Your Keys
short: Pick one spot near the door for your keys, wallet, earbuds and ID, and put them there.
why: Lost keys and earbuds cost you ten minutes on the worst possible mornings. One fixed spot and you stop looking.
how: Pick a bowl, hook, tray or corner of a shelf near where you leave.
Round up your keys, wallet, earbuds, ID and bus pass.
Drop them there every time you walk in. Already have a spot? Round up what wandered.
proof: Keys, wallet and earbuds in their spot, IDs and cards turned over.

title: Shifts on the Calendar
short: Write every shift you know about on a paper calendar or planner, with when to leave.
why: Mixing up a shift costs you money and your manager's trust. Every shift written down with a leave-by time means no guessing.
how: Get your schedule from the app, the posted sheet or your manager.
Write each shift on a paper calendar or planner with its start and end time.
Next to each one, write when you need to leave, not when the shift starts.
Set a phone alarm for each leave-by time too.
proof: Your shifts written in with leave-by times, other details covered.

title: Back Up Your Phone
short: Turn on backup for your phone's photos and contacts, then check it actually worked.
why: Phones get lost, broken and stolen. If your photos and contacts only live on the phone, one bad day deletes years of them.
how: In your phone's settings, turn on backup for photos and contacts.
Plug in on Wi-Fi and let it run. A first backup can take a few hours.
Free storage full? Copy your photos to a computer instead of paying.
Then snap a photo of your desk and find it in the backup on a computer or tablet.
proof: Your desk photo open in the backup on another screen.

title: Sort Your Chargers
short: Gather every charger and cable you own, toss the dead ones and give the rest one home.
why: Half the cables in a drawer are broken or for a phone you don't have anymore. Sorted, the one you need is where you look first.
how: Round up every charger, cable and adapter: drawers, bags, next to the bed.
Test any you're not sure about. Dead or frayed ones go to e-waste, not the trash.
Keep one at your charging spot and put the spares in one bag or box.
proof: The tangle, then sorted with the dead ones set aside.

title: Lock Down Your Email
short: Turn on 2-step verification for your main email and write the backup codes on paper.
why: Your email resets every other account you have. If someone gets into it, they can get into everything else.
how: On a laptop or computer, open your email account's security settings.
Turn on 2-step verification with your phone.
Write the backup codes on paper, keep it at home and never photograph it.
proof: The laptop screen showing 2-step is on, your email covered.

title: Clean Your Tech
short: Clean your earbuds, phone case and keyboard, with everything off and unplugged.
why: Clogged earbud mesh makes them sound quieter, and cases and keyboards collect gunk you stop seeing. Fifteen minutes fixes it.
how: Turn everything off and unplug it first.
Brush earbud mesh with a dry cotton swab or soft brush. Keep water out.
Take the phone case off, wash it with soap and water and let it dry fully.
Tip the keyboard over to shake out crumbs, then wipe with a barely damp cloth.
proof: Your earbuds and phone case before, then clean.

title: Laundry Reset
short: Fold or hang every piece of clean laundry and put it all away.
why: Clean clothes on a chair get mixed with dirty ones and washed again for nothing. Put away, you can actually see what you own.
how: Grab every clean piece: the basket, the chair, the dryer, the floor.
Hang what wrinkles, fold the rest by type.
Put it all in drawers or the closet until the basket is empty.
Put on music or a podcast and don't stop until it's done.
proof: A put-away drawer or shelf, and the empty basket.

title: Close the Kitchen
short: After dinner, get every dish done, the sink empty and the counters wiped.
why: A clean kitchen at night means breakfast isn't a cleanup job. It's also the easiest way to take something off whoever you live with.
how: Wash, dry or load every dish in the sink and on the counters.
Put food and leftovers away.
Wipe the counters, and the stovetop once it's cool.
Take the trash out if it's full.
proof: The sink and counter before, then clean.

title: Under the Bed
short: Pull everything out from under your bed, sort it and put back only what belongs.
why: Under the bed is where lost stuff, dust and old projects hide. Twenty minutes and you get the storage back and find what's missing.
how: Pull everything out onto the floor.
Trash, laundry and dishes go first.
Sweep or vacuum under there while it's empty.
Put back only what you'd actually want stored there.
proof: The pile you pulled out, then the cleared space.

title: Fix One Drawer
short: Empty one messy drawer, toss the junk and put back only what you use.
why: The junk drawer is where batteries, chargers and keys disappear. Sorted, you can find anything in it in seconds.
how: Pick the worst one: desk, nightstand or the kitchen junk drawer.
Dump it out on a table or the floor.
Toss dead pens, wrappers, broken stuff and anything you never use.
Group what's left and put it back so you can see all of it.
proof: The drawer before and after.

title: Wipe Everything Down
short: Dust and wipe every flat surface in your room: desk, shelves, windowsill, nightstand.
why: Dust builds up where you never look and makes a room feel dirty even when it's tidy. One pass with a damp cloth fixes it.
how: Get a damp cloth or paper towel.
Go top to bottom: shelves first, then the desk, then windowsills.
Clear each surface, wipe it, put things back.
Rinse the cloth as you go so you're not just moving dust around.
proof: The used cloth next to a surface you wiped.

title: Clean Your Sneakers
short: Clean one pair of shoes until they look close to new: soles, sides and laces.
why: Clean shoes make a whole outfit look put together, and they last longer when dirt isn't ground into them.
how: Knock off loose dirt and pull out the laces.
Scrub soles and sides with an old toothbrush, warm water and a little soap.
Wash the laces in the sink, then let everything air dry.
Skip the washer and dryer unless the label says it's fine.
proof: The pair before and after.

title: Sort the Paper Pile
short: Go through every loose paper in your space and sort it into recycle, keep or do.
why: Paper piles hide the permission slip, the receipt you need and the form that is due. Sorted, nothing important gets lost in there.
how: Gather every loose paper: desk, bag, drawers, floor.
Make three piles: recycle, keep, needs action.
Put the keep pile in one folder or envelope.
Put the action pile where you'll see it tomorrow morning.
proof: The pile turned over, then the three stacks with top sheets hidden.

title: Clean Up Your Files
short: 20 minutes deleting and filing what has piled up in your computer's downloads or desktop.
why: When everything lives in Downloads, finding the one file you need takes forever. A few folders and a delete pass fix that.
how: Make a few folders that fit your life: School, Work, Projects, Docs.
Start the 20:00 timer.
Delete duplicates and junk, and drag the rest into a folder.
Stop when the timer ends.
proof: Your computer folders after the timer, private names covered.

title: Map Your Week
short: Write the next 7 days on one page: every class, shift, practice, due date and appointment.
why: Things get missed when two of them land on the same day. The whole week on one page shows the crunch days before you hit them.
how: Write the next 7 days down the side of one page.
Fill in the fixed stuff: school, shifts, practice, appointments, due dates.
Find the busiest day and move one thing off it.
Pick the days laundry and errands happen.
proof: Your week on one page, anything private covered.

title: One List for Everything
short: Pull every to-do out of your head, notes app, texts and sticky notes onto one page.
why: To-dos spread across five places get forgotten in all five. One list means you stop carrying it all in your head.
how: Check your notes app, texts, school or work apps and sticky notes.
Write every open task on one sheet of paper.
Add the due date wherever there is one.
Circle the three that matter most this week.
proof: Your one list, with three circled.

title: Run the Errand
short: Do the errand you keep pushing back: a return, a drop-off, a pickup or a library book.
why: Small errands sit on the list for weeks, then cost you a late fee or a missed return window. Most take under an hour, there and back.
how: Pick the one with a deadline, or the one that's waited longest.
Get together what you need: the item, the receipt, the library card.
Walk, bike, take the bus or ride along with someone already going.
Cross it off your list when you're back.
proof: The receipt or the thing you picked up, private info covered.

title: Fill Out the Form
short: Finish the form or sign-up you've been putting off, start to finish, in one sitting.
why: Forms feel bigger than they are. Most take 15 minutes once you have the details, and they're usually blocking something you want.
how: Pick it: a permission slip, a team or club sign-up, a school or program form.
Gather every detail it asks for before you start.
Fill it out in one sitting, then submit it or put it in your bag.
Job or scholarship form? Never pay to apply.
proof: The finished form, or its confirmation on a laptop, details covered.

title: Take Over a Chore
short: Learn one household job someone else always does, then do it yourself, start to finish.
why: If you can do it yourself, you're not stuck waiting on someone else. It's easiest to learn while someone is around to show you.
how: Pick one: iron a shirt, mop the floors, vacuum the whole place, clean the windows inside.
Ask whoever usually does it to show you. For the iron, have them there the first time.
Do it yourself, start to finish, cleanup included.
proof: The result: the ironed shirt, the mopped floor, the clean window.

title: Locker Cleanout
short: Bring home everything that doesn't belong in your locker or desk at school.
why: Lockers turn into a dump for old papers, gym clothes and lost stuff. Clearing it is how you find the missing hoodie and the handout you need.
how: Before you leave school, go through your locker or desk.
Toss trash and old papers you won't need.
Bring home gym clothes, containers and anything you've been missing.
Tonight, wash what needs washing and put the rest away.
proof: Everything you brought home, laid out, papers turned over.

title: Find Your Documents
short: Find out where your ID, birth certificate and Social Security card are kept.
why: Jobs, permits and applications all ask for these, usually on short notice. Knowing where they are saves a panicked search later.
how: Make a checklist: photo ID or permit, birth certificate, Social Security card.
Find each one, or ask the adult who keeps them where they are.
Tick each one off. Never write down the numbers or where they're kept.
Keep the originals at home in one safe place, not in your bag.
proof: Your ticked checklist, with no numbers or hiding spots on it.

title: Open Your Mail
short: Open every piece of mail with your name on it and deal with each one today.
why: Unopened mail is where late fees, missed appointments and expired cards come from. Most of it takes a minute once it is open.
how: Gather every unopened envelope.
Open each one: junk to recycling, anything important to one folder.
Put every due date or appointment on your calendar.
Tear up anything with account info before it goes in the recycling.
proof: The opened envelopes, turned over so no names show.

title: Set Up Your Project Spot
short: Give your project one spot where the tools are out and ready to start.
why: If starting means digging your stuff out of a closet, you'll start less often. A ready spot cuts setup to zero.
how: Pick a corner, a shelf, a drawer or a box.
Gather everything the project uses: sketchbook, fabric, laptop, cables, notes.
Toss what's dead or used up and write down what you need to replace.
Set it up so you could start in under a minute.
proof: The spot before and after.

title: Book the Appointment
short: Book the appointment you keep putting off: dentist, doctor, eye exam, haircut or permit test.
why: Appointments wait for months because booking feels like a chore. It's one call or form, then it's on the calendar.
how: Pick the one you've put off longest.
Under 18? Book it with a parent, or get their OK and the details first.
Call or book online. Write down the date, time and what to bring.
Add it to your calendar with a reminder the day before.
proof: The date and time written down, no names or details.

title: Fridge Check
short: Clear expired and forgotten food out of the fridge, wipe the shelves and write what to buy.
why: Old food hides in the back, goes bad and makes everything smell. A quick check also stops you buying what you already have.
how: Shared or family fridge? Ask first.
Go shelf by shelf. Toss anything expired, moldy or forgotten.
Wipe the shelves, then put things back with the oldest in front.
Write a short list of what's actually running out.
proof: The fridge before, then the cleared shelves and your list.

title: Full Room Reset
short: Reset your whole room: trash and dishes out, every surface clear, floor vacuumed, bed made.
why: Doing it in pieces keeps it at 'okay'. One full reset gets it to where the 10-minute version can keep it there.
how: Take the before photo, then get the trash and dishes out first.
Clothes next: dirty in the hamper, clean put away.
Clear every surface and the floor, then vacuum or sweep and make the bed.
Take the after photo from the same spot as the before.
proof: The same view of your space, before and after.

title: Closet Cleanout
short: Pull every piece of clothing you haven't worn in a year and set it aside to donate or sell.
why: Clothes you never wear make it harder to find the ones you do. A thinner closet is easier to keep neat and shows what you actually need.
how: Go shelf by shelf, drawer by drawer.
If it doesn't fit, is damaged or you skipped it all year, it goes.
Check with whoever buys your clothes before anything leaves.
Lay it out for the photo, then bag it and put it by the door to go this week.
proof: The clothes going out, laid out before you bag them.

title: Do Your Own Laundry
short: Wash, dry, fold and put away one full load of your own clothes, start to finish.
why: If someone else does your laundry, you're one busy week away from nothing clean to wear. It's about 90 minutes, mostly waiting.
how: Sort darks from lights, empty every pocket, check labels for anything delicate.
Use the amount of detergent the cap shows, not more.
Do something else while it runs, then move it to the dryer or a rack right away.
Fold, hang and put away everything as soon as it's dry.
proof: The clean load, folded.

title: Fix One Broken Thing
short: Fix something you own that's been broken for a while, using what's already at home.
why: Broken stuff sits around for months because fixing it feels like a project. Most fixes are one how-to video and half an hour.
how: Pick one: a loose screw, split seam, missing button, stuck zipper or wobbly leg.
Skip anything that plugs in or needs tools you have never used.
Find a short how-to video and follow it step by step.
proof: The thing broken, then fixed.

title: Clean the Bathroom
short: Clean the whole bathroom: sink, counter, toilet, tub or shower, and floor.
why: It's the room everyone puts off and the one that gets gross fastest. Clean it fully once and keeping it clean is a five-minute job.
how: Put medicine and personal stuff away, then take the before photo from above.
Toss empty bottles. Spray and wipe top to bottom: counter, sink, toilet, tub or shower.
Never mix cleaning products, and open a window or run the fan.
Sweep or mop the floor last.
proof: The sink and counter from above, before and after.

title: Finally Unpack It
short: Fully unpack the bag, box or pile that's been sitting there since a trip, a move or a season.
why: A half-unpacked bag turns into a second closet you dig through. Empty it once and you get your stuff and the floor space back.
how: Pick it: the travel bag, the moving box, the bag from camp or the dorm.
Take out every single thing.
Laundry to the hamper, trash out, everything else to where it lives.
Put the empty bag away, or break the box down.
proof: The packed pile, then the empty bag or box.

title: Clear Out 20 Things
short: Find 20 things you don't use, besides clothes, and get them out of your space.
why: Stuff you never use still takes up space and makes every clean slower. Twenty things out and there's room for what you do use.
how: Look everywhere: shelves, drawers, the closet floor, under the desk.
Dead pens, old cables, broken stuff, empty boxes, things you outgrew.
Sort into trash, recycling and give away. Old batteries go to e-waste, not the trash.
Count as you go. Stop at 20, or keep going.
proof: The 20 things, sorted into piles.

title: Rearrange Your Space
short: Move your furniture so the desk, bed and storage work for how you live now.
why: Most rooms are still set up the way they were years ago. A new layout can make the desk usable and the room feel new for free.
how: Check with whoever you live with, then sketch the new layout on paper.
Desk near the light and facing away from the bed, if you can.
Empty drawers and shelves first. Never move a dresser or bookcase alone.
Clean behind and under everything while it's moved.
proof: Your space from the same corner, before and after.

title: Inbox Zero
short: On a laptop or computer, get your main inbox down to zero, or to only what still needs action.
why: An inbox with 3,000 emails is how you miss the one from school, work or an application. At zero, anything new actually gets seen.
how: Open it on a laptop or computer and archive everything older than a month.
Go through the rest: reply, act on it, archive or delete.
Anything that needs real work goes on your to-do list, then gets archived.
Set up a filter or tab so promos skip the inbox.
proof: Your inbox on a laptop at zero, email and subjects covered.

title: Weekly Reset
short: One hour to reset your week: room, laundry, bag, and the next 7 days written down.
why: Doing the small resets all at once is how the week starts clean instead of already behind.
how: Start the 60:00 timer.
Room first: trash, dishes and clothes out, bed made.
Get a load of laundry going, then empty and repack your bag for tomorrow.
Last 10 minutes: write the next 7 days on one page.
proof: Your reset space with next week written out on the desk.

title: Tie Up Loose Ends
short: 45 minutes on every small job that's been hanging over you: replies, forms, returns, bookings.
why: Replies, forms and returns each take minutes, but they sit for weeks because none feels urgent. One block clears the lot.
how: List every small job you've been putting off: the reply, the form, the return.
Start the 45:00 timer.
Shortest first. Cross each one off as it's done.
Anything left gets a day on your calendar.
proof: Your list with what you finished crossed off.

title: Write the Move
short: Write one thing you've been avoiding and the first action you'll take on it.
why: Avoiding something takes more energy than starting it. A first step with a time on it turns the dread into a task.
how: Write the one thing you keep putting off.
Under it, write a first action small enough to do in 10 minutes.
Write the time today you'll do it.
proof: The avoided thing and its first action, written down.

title: Make the Decision
short: Pick something you've been overthinking and write down what you decided.
why: Most decisions don't get better after a week of thinking. Deciding gives back the energy you've been spending going back and forth.
how: Write the choice you keep going back and forth on: a class, a design, a plan.
Write the best reason for each side, then pick one.
Write your decision and the first thing you'll do because of it.
proof: Your written decision and its first step.

title: Speak Up Once
short: Say one thing out loud in class, at practice or at work that you'd normally keep in your head.
why: The first time you talk is the hardest. Get it out early and every time after that gets easier.
how: Answer a question, add a point or suggest a better way to do something.
Do it early, before you talk yourself out of it.
Afterward, write down what you said.
proof: A note of what you said.

title: Ask the Question
short: Ask the question you think you should already know the answer to.
why: If you're lost, someone else usually is too. One question now beats guessing for the rest of the week.
how: The moment you get lost in class, at work or at practice, write the question down.
Ask it before the class, shift or session ends.
Write the answer under your question.
proof: Your question with the answer written under it.

title: Introduce Yourself
short: Introduce yourself to one person at school, work or practice you've never talked to.
why: Most people are waiting for someone else to go first. One introduction now saves months of awkward nods.
how: Pick someone you see all the time but have never talked to.
Start with something you both deal with: the class, the drill, the shift. Ask their name.
Afterward, write where you met and one thing you talked about.
proof: Where you met and what you talked about, no names.

title: Go First
short: Volunteer to go first once today: a presentation, a drill, a new task or reading out loud.
why: Going first is less pressure than waiting. There's no one to compare you to, and you're done while everyone else is still nervous.
how: Watch for the moment: a presentation, a drill, a demo, a new task.
When they ask who's first, say "Me" before you can think about it.
Write down what you went first on.
proof: A note of what you went first on.

title: Disagree Calmly
short: When you actually see something differently today, say so once, calmly, with one reason.
why: Nodding along when you disagree teaches people you don't have an opinion. One calm "I see it differently" changes that.
how: Only do it when you really see it differently, not just to argue.
Say "I see it differently" and give one reason.
Let them answer. Afterward, write their view and yours.
proof: A note with their view and yours, no names.

title: Say No Once
short: Say no to one plan or favor you'd usually go along with, and use the time for your own thing.
why: Every automatic yes comes out of time you meant for something else. A clear, polite no gets easier every time you say it.
how: Pick one: one more game, a favor, a plan you don't want. Not chores or house rules.
Say "I can't today, I'm working on something." Skip the long excuse.
Write what you said no to and what you did with the time.
proof: What you said no to and what you did instead, written.

title: Answer the Maybe
short: Turn one "maybe" you've been dodging into a clear yes or no, and send it.
why: A maybe keeps you and the other person stuck. A straight answer is kinder than leaving them hanging, even when it's no.
how: Find the invite, request or favor you haven't really answered.
Decide yes or no and write it in one sentence.
Send it or say it before the day is over.
proof: The question and your answer, written down.

title: Open It
short: Open the email, message, result or letter you've been avoiding, and write your next step.
why: Not looking doesn't change what it says. It just eats the time you'd have to deal with it.
how: Pick the one thing you've been scared to open or check.
Open it and read the whole thing once.
Write one next step and when you'll do it.
proof: Your written next step, not the message itself.

title: Draft It, Then Wait
short: Write your reply to a message that annoyed you on paper, wait an hour, then rewrite it.
why: What you send angry is usually what you end up explaining later. An hour is enough to keep the point and lose the heat.
how: Write the reply on paper, not your phone, and take the before photo.
Set a 60-minute alarm and go do something else.
Rewrite it with only what you still mean, then send that or nothing.
proof: Your first draft, then the rewrite, on paper. No names.

title: Cut the Sorry
short: Before you send your next ask, cut every "sorry", "just" and "if that's okay", then send it.
why: Starting with sorry makes a normal request sound like a favor. A plain ask gets the same answer, and people take you more seriously.
how: Write the ask on paper: to a teacher, coach, manager or group chat. Take the before photo.
Cross out every "sorry", "just", "I was wondering" and "no worries if not".
Send the plain version.
proof: Your draft before and after the cuts, on paper. No names.

title: Clean Up Your Feed
short: Mute or unfollow five accounts that make you feel behind, and follow one that teaches you a skill.
why: Highlight reels make you feel behind but never show what it took. An account that teaches you something actually helps you catch up.
how: Scroll and notice which accounts leave you feeling worse about yourself.
Mute or unfollow five. On paper, write what kind each was, not the username.
Follow one account that teaches a skill you actually want, and write it down.
proof: Your list: the five kinds you muted and the one you followed.

title: Remove the Excuse
short: Write the excuse you use most to skip something, then set up the one thing that kills it.
why: Most excuses are a setup problem: no bag packed, no plan, no space. Fix the setup and the excuse has nothing left.
how: Write the excuse you use most: "I forgot", "no time", "I didn't have my stuff".
Write the setup that fixes it: bag packed, shoes by the door, book on your pillow.
Set that one thing up now.
proof: Your excuse on paper next to the thing you set up.

title: Plan for the Nerves
short: Write 3 steps for the 10 minutes before your next test, tryout or interview, then run them once.
why: Nerves are worst in the minutes when you're just waiting. A routine you've already run gives you something to do besides overthink.
how: Pick the moment: a test, a tryout, a game, an interview, a presentation.
Write 3 steps for the 10 minutes before: slow breaths, check your stuff, your first move.
Run through all 3 once now, so they feel normal on the day.
proof: Your 3 steps, written on a card.

title: Do the Small Version
short: Take the first small step on something you've been delaying, and finish that step today.
why: Big plans stall because the first step is too big. A small version that exists beats a perfect one that doesn't.
how: Pick the thing you keep pushing back: the brand, the application, the training plan.
Shrink it to one piece: one sketch, one paragraph, one outline, one rough page.
Do that one piece today and stop when it's done.
proof: The small version, finished.

title: Prep the Hard Talk
short: Write out a conversation you've been dreading, then say your first line out loud three times.
why: Hard talks go wrong when you wing them. Knowing your first line and what you want out of it keeps you steady once it starts.
how: Write who it's with (initials only) and what you want to happen.
Write your first line, plain and short. No "sorry, but".
Write what they'll probably say and how you'll answer.
Say your first line out loud three times.
proof: Your written plan, initials only.

title: Bad Day Plan
short: Write the three steps you'll follow the next time a day goes badly.
why: On a bad day you won't think clearly, so decide now. A plan written on a normal day stops one bad moment from taking the whole week.
how: Think of your last bad day: what made it worse and what helped.
Turn those into steps, like "Eat and sleep before I reply to anyone."
Write three steps, plus one person you'll talk to if it's more than a bad day.
Keep the page where you'll find it. In a crisis, call or text 988.
proof: Your three steps and your person, initials only.

title: If It Goes Wrong
short: Write the worst realistic outcome of something you're dreading, and exactly what you'd do next.
why: Most of the fear is not knowing. Once the worst case has a plan under it, it turns into a problem you can handle.
how: Pick what's coming up: a test, a tryout, an interview, a hard ask.
Write the worst thing that could realistically happen.
Under it, write the next three things you'd do if it did.
proof: The worst case with your plan under it.

title: Goal to Daily Action
short: Pick a goal someone else decides, write the daily action that helps, and do today's.
why: You don't decide if you make the team or get the job. You decide the practice, the applications and the reps, and that's what moves it.
how: Write a goal that depends on others: a starting spot, a first sale, a job offer.
Under it, write the daily action that makes it more likely.
Do today's version and check it off.
proof: Your goal and daily action, next to what you did on it today.

title: Act on Feedback
short: Take the last real criticism of something you made and fix one part of it.
why: Feedback only counts once you use it. Fixing even one piece shows you, and whoever gave it, that you listened.
how: Think of the last note on something you made: an essay, a drawing, a resume, a project.
Pick the smallest part of it you can fix today.
Take a before photo, make the fix, then take an after photo.
proof: The work before and after the fix, any scores covered.

title: Ask How They Did It
short: Ask someone who already has what you want how they got it, and write down their steps.
why: People a few steps ahead know the shortcuts and the mistakes. Ten minutes of asking can save you months of guessing.
how: Pick someone a few steps ahead: an older teammate, a coach, a shift lead, a relative.
Ask "How did you get there, and what would you skip if you did it again?"
Write their steps and the one mistake they'd skip.
proof: Their steps and the mistake to skip, no names.

title: Own the Mistake
short: Say "that was me" about one mistake from this week, then fix what you can.
why: Owning it early keeps it small. Hiding it makes it bigger and costs you more trust than the mistake did.
how: Pick one: the missed deadline, the wrong order, the dropped ball, the thing you forgot.
Tell the person it affected: "That was me. Here's how I'll fix it."
Fix it, or the part of it you can.
proof: The fix, or a note of what you said and what you fixed.

title: Make Your Case
short: Ask for one thing you want at home with two written reasons, said once, calmly.
why: Complaining gets a no. A calm ask with real reasons gets taken seriously, even when the answer is still no this time.
how: Pick one ask: a later curfew, a fairer chore split, quiet hours, a ride.
Write two reasons it's fair and what you'll do in return.
Ask once, calmly, at a good time. If it's no, ask what would change it.
proof: Your two reasons, written before you asked.

title: Pitch the Idea
short: Tell one person the idea you've been keeping to yourself, in one or two sentences.
why: An idea that stays in your head never gets tested. One person's first question shows you what you haven't figured out yet.
how: Write the idea in one sentence: what it is and who it's for.
Tell it to one person you trust, in person or on a call.
Write down the first question they ask. That's your next thing to figure out.
proof: Your one-sentence idea and their first question.

title: Practice Out Loud
short: Practice your next presentation, speech or pitch out loud for 10 minutes before the real thing.
why: Knowing it in your head is different from saying it. The stumbles show up in practice instead of in front of people.
how: Pick what's coming up and write the main points on one card.
Start the 10:00 timer and say it out loud, start to finish, more than once.
Record audio once if you can. Write one fix on the card and run it again.
proof: Your note card with the fix written on it.

title: Invite One Person
short: Invite someone you know to study, train or build something with you, with a day and a time.
why: "We should do that sometime" never happens. A day and a time turn it into a plan, and you're less likely to skip it.
how: Pick someone working on the same class, sport or kind of project.
Ask in person or by message, and name the day, the time and a public spot.
Write the plan down when they say yes.
proof: The plan on paper: initials, day and time.

title: Check In on a Friend
short: Call or talk in person with a friend who's been quiet lately, and mostly listen.
why: When someone goes quiet, a direct question shows you noticed. One real conversation can matter more to them than you'd guess.
how: Pick the friend who's been around less lately.
Call or talk in person. Ask "How are you actually doing?"
Listen more than you talk. Ask one follow-up question.
If they mention hurting themselves, tell a trusted adult. Call or text 988.
proof: Their initials and the day you talked, nothing else.

title: After the Miss
short: After a recent loss or rejection, write what happened, one change and the date you try again.
why: Replaying it in your head just stings. Writing it down plainly turns a bad result into a plan for the next attempt.
how: Pick one recent miss: a test, a tryout, a sale, an application, a game.
Write two plain sentences on what happened. No "always", "never" or "ruined".
Write the one thing you'd change and the date you'll try again.
proof: The page: what happened, the change, the date.

title: Ask for One Fix
short: Ask your manager or shift lead for one thing you could do better, then do it next shift.
why: Most managers notice things they never say. Asking shows you take the job seriously, and the answer tells you exactly what to work on.
how: Pick a calm moment, not the rush, and not in front of the team.
Ask "What's one thing I could do better?" Don't explain or defend.
Write it down and do it on your next shift.
proof: Their one fix, written down, with your plan for next shift.

title: Tell Me About Yourself
short: Write a 30-second answer to "tell me about yourself", then say it out loud until it's smooth.
why: Interviews, new teams, new classes and first days at work all start with some version of this. A ready answer means you don't freeze.
how: Write 3 lines: what you do now, what you're good at, what you're working toward.
Cut it until it fits in 30 seconds.
Start the 10:00 timer and say it out loud, standing up, until you don't need the page.
proof: Your written answer, with the cuts.

title: One Goal This Month
short: Write one goal for this month with a number and a date, plus this week's first three actions.
why: "Get better at guitar" never ends. A number and a date tell you every week whether you're on track.
how: Pick one thing to hit by month's end: a mile time, 3 songs, a book. Not your weight.
Write it with a number and a date: "Run a mile under 8:00 by the 30th."
Write three actions for this week and the day you'll do each.
proof: Your goal, the date and this week's three actions.

title: Get Ahead of It
short: Tell whoever's counting on you about a problem before they find out, and how you'll fix it.
why: Bad news you bring early gets you options: an extension, a swap, a fix. Bad news they find on their own gets you a reputation.
how: Pick one: an assignment that'll be late, a practice you'll miss, a shift you can't make.
Write two lines: what's happening and what you'll do about it.
Tell them today, in person or by message, before the deadline.
proof: Your two lines on paper, written before you told them.

title: Rough First Version
short: Give 45 minutes to the thing you're scared will flop and make a rough first version.
why: Fear of it being bad is what keeps it at zero. A rough version gives you something real to fix instead of something to worry about.
how: Pick it: the design, the song, the business plan, the portfolio page.
Start the 45:00 timer, then put your phone in another room.
Aim for done and rough, not good. Keep going until the timer ends.
proof: What you made in the 45 minutes.

title: Make the Apology
short: Say the apology you've been putting off, in person or on a call, with no "but" in it.
why: An apology you keep putting off gets heavier every week. A real one, with no excuses, usually fixes more than you expect.
how: Write it first: what you did, that you're sorry, what you'll do now.
Cross out any "but" and any excuse.
Say it in person or on a call, not by text. Then let them answer.
proof: Your written apology, initials only.

title: Say What's Bothering You
short: Calmly tell someone what's been bothering you and what you'd like instead.
why: Holding it in leaks out as attitude. Saying it once, calmly and clearly, gives the other person a real chance to fix it.
how: Write what happened and what you'd like next time, in two lines.
Talk in person or on a call, not by text. Stick to that one thing.
Say it, then let them talk. Write down what you agreed on.
If it's bullying or you don't feel safe, take it to an adult instead.
proof: Your two lines and what you agreed on, initials only.

title: Ask Anyway
short: Pick an ask you'd normally talk yourself out of, write your odds of a yes, then ask.
why: You're turning yourself down before anyone else gets the chance. Your real odds are usually better than your guess.
how: Pick one: a deadline extension, a shift swap, a spot in the lineup, a ride.
Write your odds of a yes out of 10.
Ask plainly, once, without saying sorry first.
Tonight, write what happened next to your guess.
proof: Your odds and what happened, on paper.

title: Ask for a Second Try
short: Ask for another shot at something you messed up, and say what you'll do differently.
why: A lot of second chances only go to people who ask. Even a no shows them you care about getting it right.
how: Pick one: a retest, a redo on an essay, another go at a drill or a task at work.
Write what you'll do differently this time.
Ask in person, before class, practice or your shift.
proof: What you'll change and their answer, written down.

title: Go for the Long Shot
short: Sign up for one thing you think you won't get: a tryout, an audition, a contest or a program.
why: You can't get picked for things you never try for. A no costs you nothing you have right now.
how: Pick one that's open now: a tryout, audition, contest or program. Never pay to apply.
Under 18? Tell a parent or guardian before you sign up.
Submit it today, on paper or a computer, so you can photograph the confirmation.
proof: The confirmation on paper or a computer, personal details covered.

title: Show Up Once
short: Go to one free club, class or open gym you keep thinking about but haven't tried.
why: Thinking about it for months is harder than going once. One visit tells you if it's worth your time.
how: Pick something free, run by a school, library, rec center or community center.
Under 18? Tell a parent or guardian where you're going.
Go, stay the whole time, then write one thing for next time on the flyer.
proof: The flyer or schedule with your next-time note, address covered.

title: Ask What It Takes
short: Ask the person who decides what it would take to get the spot, role or hours you want.
why: Guessing what they want can waste months. Asking directly gets you the list, and shows them you want it.
how: Pick the goal: a starting spot, more hours, a club role, an advanced class.
Catch them after class, practice or a shift, not in front of everyone.
Ask "What would I need to show you?" and write down the list.
proof: The list of what it takes, in your handwriting.

title: Tell Someone
short: Tell one person you trust what's been stressing you out, in person or on a call.
why: Stuff you carry alone gets heavier. Saying it to one person usually makes it smaller and gets you help you didn't know was there.
how: Pick someone safe: a parent, a coach, a counselor, a close friend.
Open with "Can I tell you something that's been on my mind?"
If it's serious or you feel unsafe, pick an adult. In a crisis, call or text 988.
proof: A check mark and the date on paper. No details.

title: Go Somewhere Alone
short: Go by yourself to a free public place you'd usually only go to with friends.
why: If you only go where your friends go, they decide what you do. Going alone once shows you it's fine, and after that you can go whenever you want.
how: Pick a free public place: the library, a park, a track, a museum on a free day.
Under 18? Tell a parent or guardian where you're going and when you'll be back.
Stay at least 30 minutes and do one thing there: read, train, draw, explore.
proof: Something from there: a book, the track, the view. No people.
